stops.name: Rome, the Chamber, the Aventine Secession
stops.campa: Some hundred and thirty opposition deputies, Socialists, Popolari and Liberals together, walk out of the Chamber in what will be called the Aventine Secession, refusing to sit again beside men implicated in Matteotti's murder until the king dismisses Mussolini. They wait on constitutional propriety and royal conscience; neither arrives. By emptying the one chamber that might have restrained him, the boycott instead hands Mussolini the year of relative quiet he needs to close every remaining door behind it.

stops.name: Rome, the Chamber, the speech that begins the dictatorship
stops.campa: Before a Chamber still half in shock, Mussolini ends six months of crisis at a single stroke: he alone, he declares, assumes the political, moral and historical responsibility for everything that has happened, dares the deputies to impeach him, and promises the country will be set in order within forty-eight hours. Within days opposition newspapers are shut, meeting halls sealed, over a hundred dissidents arrested. The speech is remembered ever after as the true founding date of the Fascist dictatorship.
stops.quote: I declare here, before this Assembly and before the entire Italian people, that I alone assume the political, moral, and historical responsibility for everything that has happened.
stops.quote_source: Speech to the Chamber of Deputies, Rome, 3 January 1925

stops.name: Rome, the Lateran Palace, the Pacts signed
stops.campa: At noon in the Lateran Palace, Mussolini for the Kingdom of Italy and Cardinal Gasparri for Pope Pius XI sign the treaty, concordat and financial convention that close the fifty-nine-year Roman Question. Vatican City is recognized as a sovereign state the size of a park; Catholicism is restored as Italy's state religion. The Church that once excommunicated the men who took Rome from the Pope now blesses the regime that rules it; church bells ring across the peninsula, and the once fiercely anticlerical Duce is hailed by the faithful as a man of Providence.

stops.name: Littoria, the battle of the marshes and the wheat
stops.campa: On the reclaimed Pontine Marshes, drained at last of the malarial water that has ruled this coast since Roman times, Mussolini inaugurates the new town of Littoria, raised by decree in under eight months. He poses shirtless with a scythe for the newsreel cameras of the wheat battle, threshing grain beside veteran settler-families each given a farmhouse, a cow and a plough. It is fascism's proudest boast of creation rather than conquest, though the older wetland life of the coast disappears beneath the new farms.

stops.name: Rome, Palazzo Venezia, war declared on Ethiopia
stops.campa: From the balcony of the Palazzo Venezia, before a piazza packed and relayed by radio across the whole peninsula, Mussolini announces the invasion of Ethiopia, an old colonial grudge dressed as civilizing mission and answer to League of Nations sanctions he calls an unjust siege of a proud people. Within hours Marshal De Bono's forces cross from Eritrea. Over the following months, on Mussolini's own written authorization, mustard gas banned by treaty since 1925 will be dropped on Ethiopian troops and villages alike to break a resistance the conventional advance cannot.

stops.name: Rome, Palazzo Venezia, the empire proclaimed
stops.campa: Addis Ababa fallen and Haile Selassie fled into exile, Mussolini returns to the same balcony to proclaim the birth of the Italian Empire: Victor Emmanuel III is hailed Emperor of Ethiopia, Badoglio made Duke of Addis Ababa, and Mussolini himself takes the title First Marshal of the Empire. Enormous crowds, primed by fifteen years of propaganda, roar their approval below him. It is the zenith of his popularity, the hour Fascist Italy believes it has truly refounded Rome.
stops.quote: After fifteen centuries, the empire reappears on the fateful hills of Rome.
stops.quote_source: Balcony address, Palazzo Venezia, Rome, 9 May 1936

stops.name: Milan, Piazza del Duomo, the Axis speech
stops.campa: Speaking in Milan on the anniversary of the March on Rome, Mussolini names the new understanding with Nazi Germany, agreed weeks earlier, an axis around which the rest of Europe might yet be induced to revolve, not a diaphragm dividing the continent but a line of collaboration open to all. The word outlives the speech and gives the coming alliance its name. He still imagines Italy the senior, civilizing partner in the pairing, steering an ally rather than serving a master, an illusion the following nine years will strip from him piece by piece.
stops.quote: This Berlin-Rome line is not a diaphragm but rather an axis around which all those European states with a will to collaboration and peace can also assemble.
stops.quote_source: Speech in the Piazza del Duomo, Milan, 1 November 1936

stops.name: Rome, the Manifesto della razza and the racial laws
stops.campa: To prove Fascist Italy's loyalty to its German ally, Mussolini's government publishes the Manifesto della razza, declaring Italians a race apart and the country's Jews foreign to the Italian nation. Through the autumn the racial laws follow, stripping Italian Jews, among them decorated veterans and party members of the first hour, of citizenship, property, profession and schooling. Mussolini, who had mocked Nazi race theory as recently as a few years before, signs the laws that make Fascist Italy an active partner in Hitler's antisemitism rather than its reluctant guest.

stops.name: Munich, the four-power conference
stops.campa: Summoned by Chamberlain's plea and Hitler's threat of war over the Sudetenland, Mussolini proposes a four-power conference and flies to Munich to broker it, arriving as the one man both Hitler and the Western democracies will still hear. The agreement drafted overnight, and signed by Hitler, Chamberlain, Daladier and himself, hands Hitler the Sudetenland without a shot fired. He returns to a Rome that cheers him in the streets as the savior of European peace, a peace that will not survive another twelve months.

stops.name: Rome, awaiting the Pact of Steel
stops.campa: While Ciano and Ribbentrop sign in Berlin, Mussolini waits in Rome for word of the alliance he has named himself, discarding his first choice, Pact of Blood, for the harder-edged Pact of Steel. The treaty binds Italy to support Germany in any war it starts, offensive or defensive, with no exit clause and no requirement of consultation. Mussolini privately tells his own generals Italy will not be ready for a general war before 1943 at the earliest, a caveat Hitler will not trouble himself to honor.

stops.name: Rome, Palazzo Venezia, the declaration of war
stops.campa: With France already beaten and Britain apparently soon to follow, Mussolini judges the moment safe to enter a war he fears missing rather than one he is prepared to fight. From the Palazzo Venezia balcony he tells the massed crowd that an hour marked by destiny is striking in the sky of the fatherland, the hour of irrevocable decisions. The army he sends within weeks against a collapsing France, and soon after into Greece and North Africa, will expose within months how little of the imperial machine built through the 1930s was ever real.
stops.quote: An hour marked by destiny is striking in the sky of our fatherland. The hour of irrevocable decisions.
stops.quote_source: Declaration of war, Palazzo Venezia balcony, Rome, 10 June 1940

stops.name: Rome, the Grand Council, the Grandi motion
stops.campa: With Sicily invaded and Rome itself bombed for the first time, the Fascist Grand Council meets for the first time in years through the night of the twenty-fourth into the early hours of the twenty-fifth. Dino Grandi's motion, asking the king to resume full constitutional command of the armed forces, passes nineteen votes to seven after nine exhausting hours in which Mussolini argues but does not fight. He leaves believing the vote merely advisory to the crown. It is, in law and in fact, the instrument by which his own creature ends twenty-one years of dictatorship.
